title: Optimizing Kitchen Waste Supernatant as a Growth Medium for Scenedesmus sp. and Its Efficacy in Multi‐Taxa Zooplankton Rearing
content:
ABSTRACT

The development of low-cost and sustainable live-feed production systems remains a major challenge in aquaculture. This study investigated the potential of digested kitchen waste supernatant (DKWS) as an alternative nutrient source for microalgal cultivation and its subsequent application in zooplankton production. In the first experiment, Scenedesmus sp. was cultured in different DKWS concentrations (5%–35%), with Bold basal medium (BBM) used as the control. Algal growth performance, biomass production, pigment content and nutrient removal efficiency were evaluated to determine the optimal substrate concentration. Maximum algal density and biomass (1.47 g L−1) were obtained at 15% DKWS, which also supported efficient nitrogen and phosphorus removal (∼90%) from the culture medium. In the second experiment, the cultured Scenedesmus sp. was used as feed for the four zooplankton taxa—copepods (Diaptomus and Cyclops) and cladocerans (Moina and Diaphanosoma)—under different dietary regimes, including the microalgae (Scenedesmus sp.), baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), DKWS and their combinations. Zooplankton reared on algal-based diets, particularly the algae–DKWS combination, achieved significantly higher population densities and higher protein content compared with non-algal diets, whereas lipid content did not differ significantly among the treatments. Distinct taxon-specific patterns were observed within the mixed zooplankton communities, with Diaptomus showing the highest abundance under algal feeding, whereas Cyclops showed the highest abundance with the algae–DKWS combination, and Moina and Diaphanosoma showed higher abundances under algal-based diets with or without DKWS. These responses may reflect the combined effects of dietary conditions and interactions among co-cultured taxa. The results demonstrate that kitchen-waste-derived nutrients can effectively sustain microalgal growth and enhance zooplankton productivity, supporting the potential of this approach for sustainable live-feed production in aquaculture systems.
